title: Luke 5:12–26
context: Jesus cleanses a man full of leprosy with a touch and a word, then sends him to the priest as the law commands. As crowds grow, He withdraws to pray. Later, before Pharisees and teachers from across the land, friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof. Seeing their faith, Jesus forgives his sins and heals him to prove that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive. Both traditions see here Jesus’ divine authority and compassion.

verses.text: While he was in one of the cities, behold, there was a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, saying, “Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean.”
verses.arminianNotes: A man full of leprosy says, “Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean.” Arminian readers see humble faith that trusts Jesus’ power and appeals to His willingness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a plea that rests entirely on Jesus’ will. The man does not doubt Jesus’ power, only whether he will be chosen for mercy.

verses.text: He stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I want to. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus touches him and says, “I want to.” Arminian readers see Jesus’ willingness as a revelation of God’s heart toward the suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jesus’ sovereign will and compassion together. His touch reverses uncleanness rather than contracting it.

verses.text: He commanded him to tell no one, “But go your way and show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing according to what Moses commanded, for a testimony to them.”
verses.arminianNotes: He tells him to show himself to the priest as Moses commanded. Arminian readers see Jesus honoring the law and restoring the man to community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the law’s witness to Jesus’ authority. The cleansing is to be a testimony to them.

verses.text: But the report concerning him spread much more, and great multitudes came together to hear and to be healed by him of their infirmities.
verses.arminianNotes: The report spreads, and crowds come. Arminian readers see the spread of interest in Jesus. Jesus’ fame grows as people seek both teaching and healing, which Luke keeps together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jesus’ fame grows even when He seeks restraint. Luke shows that the crowds come for healing as well as for hearing, and Jesus meets both needs.

verses.text: But he withdrew himself into the desert and prayed.
verses.arminianNotes: He withdraws to the desert to pray. Arminian readers see Jesus’ dependence on the Father as a model for disciples. Even with crowds pressing in, He makes room for communion with the Father.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Luke’s frequent emphasis on Jesus at prayer at key moments. His withdrawal is not escape but renewal for the mission.

verses.text: On one of those days, he was teaching; and there were Pharisees and teachers of the law sitting by who had come out of every village of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. The power of the Lord was with him to heal them.
verses.arminianNotes: Pharisees and teachers of the law sit by, and the Lord’s power is present to heal. Arminian readers see God’s power available in the moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the presence of religious leaders setting up a test of Jesus’ authority.

verses.text: Behold, men brought a paralyzed man on a cot, and they sought to bring him in to lay before Jesus.
verses.arminianNotes: Men bring a paralyzed man on a cot and try to lay him before Jesus. Arminian readers see love and determination bringing someone who cannot come alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see friends acting in faith for another. God often uses the care of others to bring people into Christ’s presence.

verses.text: Not finding a way to bring him in because of the multitude, they went up to the housetop and let him down through the tiles with his cot into the middle before Jesus.
verses.arminianNotes: Blocked by the crowd, they lower him through the roof tiles. Arminian readers see persistent faith that overcomes obstacles rather than giving up.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see bold faith that refuses to be stopped by the crowd. Luke’s detail of tiles fits a house type familiar to his readers.

verses.text: Seeing their faith, he said to him, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Seeing their faith, Jesus says, “Your sins are forgiven.” Arminian readers note that Jesus responds to the faith of the friends, and many see the man’s faith included too.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the friends’ faith honored while forgiveness itself is Jesus’ sovereign gift.

verses.text: The scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins, but God alone?”
verses.arminianNotes: The leaders ask, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Arminian readers see the leaders rightly recognize forgiveness as God’s prerogative. Their question is right; their conclusion about Jesus is wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question pointing to Jesus’ divine identity. If only God forgives, Jesus’ words either blaspheme or reveal who He is.

verses.text: But Jesus, perceiving their thoughts, answered them, “Why are you reasoning so in your hearts?
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus perceives their thoughts. Arminian readers see His insight into human hearts. Jesus addresses hidden objections directly and openly rather than ignoring them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see divine knowledge displayed. Only God searches hearts, and Jesus does so here.

verses.text: Which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Arise and walk’?
verses.arminianNotes: Which is easier to say? Arminian readers see Jesus inviting them to think about visible and invisible acts. Saying sins are forgiven cannot be checked; saying arise can be.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the logic: the visible healing will confirm the invisible forgiveness. Jesus chooses the harder test to vindicate the unseen word.

verses.text: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,” he said to the paralyzed man, “I tell you, arise, take up your cot, and go to your house.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Son of Man has authority to forgive sins. Arminian readers see Jesus claiming divine authority. He links forgiveness and healing so the crowd can see His authority at work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Daniel 7 behind Son of Man, a figure given authority and dominion. The phrase on earth stresses that God’s authority to forgive is now present in Jesus’ ministry.

verses.text: Immediately he rose up before them, and took up that which he was laying on, and departed to his house, glorifying God.
verses.arminianNotes: He rises, takes his cot, and goes home glorifying God. Arminian readers see grateful response to grace. Healing leads straight to worship, which Luke often stresses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a life restored and God glorified. His glorifying God shows that the gift points back to the giver.

verses.text: Amazement took hold on all, and they glorified God. They were filled with fear, saying, “We have seen strange things today.”
verses.arminianNotes: Amazement and fear fill all. Arminian readers see awe at God’s work. Luke records amazement, praise, and fear together in response to Jesus.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wonder that does not yet amount to understanding. Strange things today hints that the crowd senses something new without yet grasping it.
